beats.lead: Discord wasn't built as a chat app for gamers.
beats.text: It was the second product from a team whose first was a video game that flopped.
beats.note: That game was Fates Forever, a mobile MOBA released in 2014.

beats.name: Jason Citron
beats.role: Sold his previous company, mobile gaming platform OpenFeint, to Japan's GREE for $104 million in cash — then used the fresh start to found Hammer & Chisel and build a game.

beats.lead: Fates Forever never found its audience.
beats.text: While building it, the team kept hitting the same wall: voice and text chat for gamers hadn't meaningfully improved in a decade.
beats.note: TeamSpeak and Skype were still what most players were stuck with.

beats.lead: So they built the tool instead of another game.
beats.text: Discord launched publicly in May 2015, aimed straight at the problem Fates Forever had run into.
beats.note: Same team, same instinct, a completely different product.

beats.context: Discord's user count by the end of 2017 — up from 3 million less than two years earlier, gaining roughly 1.5 million new users a week.

beats.line: A failed MOBA's real legacy: the voice chat its own players never got to use.
